ZNF217 enhances the transcriptional activity of its downstream effector PROM2, thereby suppressing ferroptosis and promoting cell survival. Functional assays demonstrate that ZNF217 silencing markedly amplifies ferroptotic features, whereas ZNF217 overexpression partially alleviates ferroptosis-induced cellular damage. Building on these findings, we established a drug screening system based on ZNF217 expression and identified the compound RSL3 from a panel of 13 ferroptosis inducers, which potently suppresses ZNF217 expression. Further investigations revealed that combined treatment with RSL3 and the AR antagonist enzalutamide produced a synergistic antitumor response in cellular and animal models, accompanied by marked attenuation of AR/ZNF217/PROM2 pathway activity and reduced tumor burden. Collectively, these findings identify AR/ZNF217/PROM2 signaling as a central determinant of ferroptotic vulnerability in prostate cancer and suggest that targeting this pathway may enhance sensitivity to AR inhibition, providing a molecular rationale for combination therapy in castration-resistant prostate cancer.

title: Dual downregulation of HRK and BAD promotes BCL-xL-mediated docetaxel resistance in prostate cancer
abstract: Prostate cancer is the second most common malignancy in men. For patients who present metastatic disease, androgen deprivation therapy is the standard of care. Despite significant initial responses to anti-androgenic therapy, almost all patients progress to an incurable metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, facing a significant therapeutic challenge. Docetaxel is a taxane that improves response rates in these patients, but its efficacy is limited due to the development of resistance, which can be mediated through anti-apoptotic adaptations. Dynamic BH3 profiling is a functional assay that can anticipate tumors’ anti-apoptotic adaptation to treatment and guide the use of specific inhibitors such as BH3 mimetics or PROTACs. In this study, we elucidate that BCL-xL is the major pro-survival protein in prostate cancer cell lines after docetaxel treatment, which can be reverted using BH3 mimetics or PROTAC strategies against this protein. We also describe for the first time that the downregulation of HRK and BAD sensitizer BH3-only proteins due to docetaxel treatment leads to BCL-xL mediated resistance in prostate cancer cells. Finally, we introduce a new functional technology that detects mitochondrial permeabilization, enabling successful testing of this therapeutic combination directly in patient‑derived prostate cancer cells.

title: The role of m6A reader YTHDF2 in lymphangiogenesis via RNF43/WNT5B in oral squamous cell carcinoma
abstract: Abstract Lymphangiogenesis significantly contributes to poor prognosis and reduced survival in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) patients due to lymphatic metastasis. Despite the critical role of N6-methyladenosine (m 6 A)—the most abundant eukaryotic mRNA modification—its influence on OSCC lymphangiogenesis and metastasis remains poorly understood. This study identifies YTHDF2, a key m 6 A reader protein, as markedly upregulated in OSCC and strongly correlated with advanced nodal staging (N-staging). In vitro experiments revealed that YTHDF2 enhances OSCC cell migration and invasion while promoting tube formation and migration in human lymphatic endothelial cells (HLECs). In vivo experiments showed that silencing YTHDF2 reduced lymphatic vessel density in orthotopic tumors and suppressed cervical lymph node metastasis. Mechanistically, integrated RNA-seq and m 6 A-seq data linked YTHDF2-regulated genes to the WNT pathway. YTHDF2 directly binds m 6 A-modified RNF43 mRNA, accelerating its decay and upregulating WNT5B expression. Our findings indicate that WNT5B serves as an important contributor to lymphangiogenesis and lymphatic metastasis in OSCC. These findings elucidate the role of YTHDF2 in OSCC metastasis via m 6 A dependent regulation of the RNF43-WNT5B axis. In addition, WNT5B appears to contribute to lymphangiogenesis signaling, and these findings point toward the YTHDF2-RNF43-WNT5B pathway as a subject of interest for future therapeutic exploration in OSCC.

title: CD44v5 promotes triple-negative breast cancer cisplatin resistance by enhancing IL-4/IL-4Rα/STAT3 pathway and stabilizing membranous SLC7A11
abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive subtype of breast cancer with limited therapeutic options, and the development of chemoresistance remains a major challenge for effective treatment. Our findings reveal that the CD44 variant isoform CD44v5 plays a crucial role in TNBC cisplatin resistance. Analyses of clinical samples, bioinformatic data, and cellular experiments demonstrated that CD44v5 was highly expressed in TNBC and correlated with tumor-associated macrophage (TAM) infiltration and poor therapeutic response. Mechanistically, TAMs enhanced cisplatin resistance through CD44v5-dependent mechanisms by releasing interleukin-4 (IL-4). CD44v5 amplified the IL-4/IL-4Rα/STAT3 signaling pathway, which upregulated SLC7A11 expression and inhibited ferroptosis. In addition, CD44v5 stabilized SLC7A11 on the cell membrane by preventing its internalization, which reduced reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation and promoted TNBC ferroptosis resistance. Furthermore, in vivo studies demonstrated that CD44v5 knockdown significantly enhanced the antitumor efficacy of cisplatin through suppression of SLC7A11 expression and induction of ferroptosis, accompanied by decreased IL-4Rα expression and reduced TAM infiltration. These findings indicate that CD44v5 contributes to cisplatin resistance by both reinforcing IL-4/IL-4Rα/STAT3 signaling and maintaining SLC7A11 membrane stability, highlighting CD44v5 as a potential therapeutic target for overcoming chemoresistance in TNBC.

title: A novel combinatorial treatment for Neurofibromatosis type 1 tumours revealed through cross-species genetic analysis
abstract: Abstract Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is a multisystem genetic disorder associated with a wide range of symptoms, including the formation of tumours along nerves. These tumours can affect nerve function, leading to pain and loss of sensory or motor capacity. Drug treatments are currently limited, and relatively few new targets have emerged for NF1 tumours despite intensive research. Therefore, new drugs to target NF1 -deficient tumour cells are urgently required. Here, we have used a cross-species screening strategy combined with bioinformatic analysis to identify candidates with a high chance of successful translation to humans. First, we used data from a synthetic lethal screen performed in Drosophila cells to identify novel drug targets of NF1 . Then, we performed statistical enrichment analysis of the screen results to identify further candidate targets that were not conserved between Drosophila and humans and could not have been found in the screen. We identified and validated hTERT as a synthetic lethal partner gene to NF1 with high potential as a therapeutic drug target, using the FDA-approved inhibitor azidothymidine (AZT). The lethal effect of AZT was validated in plexiform neurofibroma NF1 -deficient human cell lines and NF1 -deficient malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour cells. The effect of AZT was also conserved in vivo, highlighting the translational potential; treatment of mice with AZT inhibited NF1 mutant xenograft growth to the same extent as the current clinically approved MEK inhibitor, selumetinib. Finally, we show that combined treatment with AZT and selumetinib resulted in a further synergistic reduction in NF1 -deficient human cell viability. In conclusion, AZT represents a promising novel therapeutic for the treatment of NF1 tumours, either alone or in combination with selumetinib.

title: Stanniocalcin 1 contributes to glioma stem cells phenotypic plasticity through NOTCH1/STAT3/GFPT2 axis
abstract: Glioma stem cells (GSCs) are key drivers of glioblastoma (GBM) tumorigenesis, invasion, therapy resistance, and recurrence and exhibit remarkable phenotypic plasticity. Stanniocalcin 1 (STC1) has been implicated in tumor progression and cancer stemness; however, its role and the molecular mechanisms through which it shapes GSC plasticity and malignant traits remain poorly understood. Here, transcriptomic RNA sequencing identified STC1 as a malignancy-associated gene enriched in GBM and mesenchymal (MES)-like GSCs. Comprehensive bioinformatic analyses further validated that STC1 was highly expressed in MES-like GBM/GSCs and closely associated with poor patient survival. Functional studies revealed that STC1 promoted multiple malignant properties of GSCs, including self-renewal, migration, invasion, tumorigenicity, and cellular plasticity. Conversely, STC1 silencing attenuated these effects. Mechanistically, STC1 activated the NOTCH1/STAT3 signaling cascade, leading to transcriptional upregulation of GFPT2, a key rate-limiting enzyme of the hexosamine biosynthetic pathway. This subsequently enhanced global O-GlcNAcylation, including modification of P65, thereby facilitating GSC plasticity and malignant progression. Genetic and pharmacological interventions targeting this signaling axis effectively mitigated the oncogenic effects driven by STC1. In conclusion, our study reveals that STC1 is a key regulator of GSC phenotypic plasticity and aggressiveness through the NOTCH1/STAT3/GFPT2/O-GlcNAcylation pathway. These results provide new mechanistic insights into GBM progression and suggest that targeting STC1-associated signaling networks may represent a potential therapeutic strategy for GBM.

title: Compartmentalisation of death receptor signalling in cancer
abstract: Abstract Death Receptor (DR) ligands, such as CD95L and TRAIL, are historically considered as key players of tumour immunosurveillance through their ability to induce cell death. Yet, depending on the cellular context, their corresponding DR, CD95 and TRAILR1/2, also initiate various non-cytotoxic pathways and cellular functions and display multiple pro-tumoural functions across various cancer types. To unleash the full potential of the therapeutic targeting of DR signalling, it is therefore essential to understand the molecular mechanisms that tip the scales between their anti- and pro-tumoural effects. DR signalling is physiologically tightly regulated, and hence widely dysregulated in cancer, at multiple steps. Herein, focusing on the DR CD95, TRAILR1/2 and TNFR1, we first summarise their main signalling regulatory steps and therapeutic strategies developed for their targeting in cancer. Then, we focus on the emerging and sometimes controversial roles of cellular compartmentalisation in the regulation of DR signalling in cancer.

title: NKCC1 as a regulator of stemness and redox balance in colorectal cancer
abstract: Abstract Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl − cotransporter 1 (encoded by SLC12A2 ) is a solute carrier overexpressed in colorectal cancer (CRC), but its functional role remains unclear. Here, we identify NKCC1 as a marker of normal intestinal stem cells, supported by its crypt-base localization, single-cell transcriptomics, and patient-derived organoids, while analyses of public colorectal cancer single-cell datasets further link NKCC1 expression to cancer stem cell populations. Surprisingly, analysis of CRC patient datasets revealed that tumors with lower SLC12A2 expression were associated with poorer relapse-free survival. By stably knocking down NKCC1 in cell lines and organoids, we demonstrate enhanced expression of stemness markers, altered oxidative stress pathways, and increased radioresistance. In contrast, pharmacological inhibition with bumetanide activates AKT/mTORC1 signaling, elevates reactive oxygen species (ROS), and sensitizes cells to oxidative stress. Together, these results highlight NKCC1 as a dual regulator of stemness and redox homeostasis, supporting its role as a potential key player in colorectal carcinogenesis.

title: Acrolein- thioredoxin 1- p38 signaling drives neutrophil-mediated immunosuppression and glioblastoma progression
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is a highly aggressive type of brain tumor characterized by diffuse infiltration and a profoundly immunosuppressive microenvironment in which polymorphonuclear myeloid-derived suppressor cells (PMN-MDSCs) derived from neutrophils play a key role. In this study, we investigated how acrolein, a reactive aldehyde that accumulates under oxidative stress, modulates neutrophil redox regulation and promotes their polarization toward an immunosuppressive phenotype. We found that acrolein covalently modifies thioredoxin 1 (TRX1) at Cys35, impairing its activity and activating the apoptosis signal-regulating kinase 1 (ASK1)–p38 signaling cascade. This redox disruption drives neutrophils toward an MDSC-like state, characterized by increased expression of LOX-1 and Arg-1, enhanced COX-2/PGE₂ production, and suppressed CD8⁺ T-cell proliferation. Importantly, pharmacological inhibition of p38 or scavenging of acrolein reversed these effects, restored CD8⁺ T-cell infiltration, and significantly reduced glioma growth in murine models. Clinically, increased frequencies of Acr⁺CD15⁺ and p-p38⁺CD15⁺ neutrophils were associated with decreased CD8⁺ T-cell infiltration and poor patient survival. Mechanistically, this study identifies TRX1 Cys35 as a critical target of acrolein and establishes the activity of the acrolein–TRX1–p38 axis as a novel link between oxidative stress and neutrophil-mediated immunosuppression in GBM. Therefore, targeting this pathway may represent a promising strategy to restore antitumor immunity and counteract immune evasion in glioblastoma.

title: Catechol-O-methyltransferase bioactivation of the imiqualine EAPB02303 generates EAPB04303, a broadly active anti-leukemic agent in acute myeloid leukemia
abstract: Imiqualines, analogs of the immunomodulatory drug Imiquimod, display potent anticancer properties. The first-generation EAPB0503 demonstrated high efficacy and selectivity against acute myeloid leukemia (AML) expressing mutant nucleophosmin-1 (NPM1c). The second-generation EAPB02303 was more potent and exhibited broader activity against AML with various mutations in vitro. However, the in vivo survival advantage was limited only to NPM1c AML xenograft mice. The enzyme catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) was implicated in the bioactivation of EAPB02303 in pancreatic cancer. In this study, we demonstrated that COMT is highly expressed in AML cells, and converts EAPB02303 into an active metabolite, EAPB04303. This metabolite had lower IC50s than its parent compound, and a similar mechanism of action through inhibition of PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway. Furthermore, EAPB04303 significantly increased mitochondrial stress in NPM1c AML cells, presumably explaining their higher sensitivity to this metabolite. In vivo, EAPB04303 attenuated leukemic burden and significantly extended survival in all tested AML cell-derived and patient-derived xenograft mouse models. These findings poise EAPB04303 as a promising candidate for AML therapy.

title: Deacetylation-dependent stabilization of VASH2 drives YAP activation leading to colorectal cancer progression and chemoresistance
abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a common and fatal malignancy, with chemoresistance posing a formidable challenge. Understanding the mechanisms driving CRC progression and chemoresistance is essential for new therapy development. Although vasohibin-2 (VASH2) is known for its pro-angiogenic role, its non-angiogenic functions in CRC are less well understood. This study aimed to clarify VASH2’s role and mechanisms in CRC progression and chemosensitivity, and to delineate the regulatory pathway controlling its expression. Analysis of public databases and RNA sequencing data revealed that VASH2 is significantly upregulated in CRC and correlated with poor chemosensitivity. Increased VASH2 expression was also confirmed in clinical CRC tissue samples. Based on these findings, stable VASH2-knockdown CRC cell lines were established. In vitro and in vivo assays demonstrated that VASH2 knockdown suppressed malignant growth and increased chemosensitivity. Mechanistically, VASH2 promoted α-tubulin detyrosination, which is associated with reduced YAP phosphorylation and degradation. Furthermore, histone deacetylase 10 (HDAC10) was identified as a critical stabilizer of VASH2, inhibiting its proteasomal degradation and increasing VASH2 levels. Collectively, these findings indicate that elevated VASH2 enhances α-tubulin detyrosination and increases YAP protein levels, thereby driving CRC progression and chemoresistance. Furthermore, HDAC10 enhances VASH2 stability by preventing its proteasomal degradation, leading to its upregulation in CRC. These results reveal a novel VASH2-driven oncogenic pathway and provide a foundation for targeting VASH2 in CRC therapy. Image illustrating the mechanism of the HDAC10-VASH2 axis influences YAP activation to regulate CRC growth and chemosensitivity. Our findings reveal that HDAC10-mediated deacetylation of VASH2 at lysine 281 suppresses its proteasomal degradation, thereby stabilizing VASH2 expression in CRC. This upregulation enhances α-tubulin detyrosination, facilitates YAP activation, and ultimately contributes to accelerating tumor progression and reducing chemosensitivity.

title: Estrogen stimulation induces centrosome amplification through estrogen receptor alpha-mediated DNA damage
abstract: Abstract Estrogen plays a critical role in breast cancer development. Estrogen exposure during puberty is implicated in the emergence of precancerous mammary cells exhibiting chromosomal alterations. The presence of two centrosomes at the onset of mitosis promotes accurate chromosome segregation; thus, centrosome amplification can cause chromosomal instability. Here, we revealed that estrogen receptor alpha (ERα) activated by estrogen induces DNA damage, causing centrosome amplification via DNA damage response signaling. Under estrogen stimulation, ERα generates DNA double-strand breaks, which activate polo-like kinase 1 (PLK1) at the centrosomes. Activated PLK1 induces premature centriole disengagement, resulting in centrosome amplification. In addition to full-length ERα, which is the major isoform, the shorter isoform ERα46 also induced DNA damage, resulting in centrosome amplification under estrogen stimulation. Our results present a potential mechanism by which estrogen induces chromosomal alterations. This study reveals a novel role for estrogen stimulation in breast cancer development.

title: Metabolic and DNA-based assays provide equally reliable measures of cell viability across experimental conditions
abstract: Accurately and reliably assessing cell viability is a fundamental necessity in biomedical research. However, many cytotoxic compounds used in cancer research have both on- and off-target effects on cellular metabolism, which may confound metabolism-based cell viability assessments, whereas DNA- and protein–stain-based methods are thought to be less susceptible to this limitation. This study aimed to compare the performance of the metabolic assay CellTiter-Blue (CTB) with the DNA-staining assay Crystal Violet (CV) after treatment with cytotoxic drugs with and without off-target effects, mitochondria-inhibiting compounds, and diaphorase inhibitors in three esophageal adenocarcinoma cell lines, as a formal comparison of the two methods has not yet been established. CTB and CV returned highly comparable half-maximal inhibitory concentrations at 72 h, with strong correlations between readouts for nearly all tested compounds. Gene and protein expression analysis of cell lines with differential CTB reduction capacity identified NQO1 as the diaphorase enzyme responsible for the CTB reaction. CTB underestimated cell viability by up to 53% compared with CV after short-term pharmacological diaphorase inhibition, but there was no difference for any of the other tested compounds in this timeframe. This was confirmed functionally by an shRNA-mediated knockdown of NQO1, resulting in a significantly reduced capacity to metabolize CTB without compensatory changes in the expression of other diaphorases. As CTB and CV results were comparable at 72 h after treatment with NQO1 inhibitors, we conclude that CTB is a robust method across nearly all inhibitors and in most realistically applied timeframes.

title: Dynamic plasticity of cancer-associated fibroblasts during tumor progression: emerging concepts
abstract: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are a predominant cellular component of the stroma in many solid cancers and play critical roles in cancer progression and therapeutic response. Recent single-cell transcriptomic analyses identified different subpopulations of CAFs, including myofibroblastic CAFs, inflammatory CAFs and antigen-presenting CAFs. Pseudotime analyses reveal that CAFs are highly plastic, switching in response to changing tumor-derived cues and microenvironmental signals. While many reviews have described CAF heterogeneity and functional diversity as relatively static features, emerging evidence suggests that CAF identity evolves dynamically during tumor progression. In this review, we specifically emphasize the dynamic heterogeneity and plasticity of CAFs. By integrating insights from multiple human cancer types, including breast, liver, lung and pancreatic cancers, this review highlights how cancer cells shape the CAF phenotype that sustains tumor progression in turn. Understanding the complex intercellular dialogue in the tumor microenvironment and deciphering the molecular mechanisms underlying CAF plasticity open new prospects for targeting the “right CAF subset at the right time” to improve patient prognosis.

title: Histone H3K18 lactylation fuels MTHFD2-driven SAM biosynthesis to promote SPINT2 promoter hypermethylation and ovarian cancer progression
abstract: Lactate-dependent histone modification represents a novel histone mark that links glycolytic metabolites with the epigenetic process of lactylation. Metabolic reprogramming and epigenetic alterations are pivotal in cancer progression. However, the specific role of histone lactylation in ovarian cancer (OC) remains unclear. Histone lactylation in OC was measured by immunoblotting and immunohistochemistry. Lactylation was inhibited using glycolysis inhibitors and LDHA knockdown. H3K18la target genes were identified by CUT&Tag and RNA-seq, with MTHFD2 validated at the chromatin binding, transcriptional, and protein expression level. Then, potential downstream genes were selected from genome-wide DNA methylation changes by whole-genome sequencing following MTHFD2 knockdown. OC specimens showed significantly higher H3K18 lactylation than the normal ovary. Glycolysis inhibition and LDHA gene knockdown effectively corrected the aberrant lactylation, thereby impeding OC progression both in vivo and in vitro. H3K18la enrichment at the MTHFD2 promoter activated its transcription, contributing to OC pathogenesis. Increased MTHFD2 expression enhanced SPINT2 promoter methylation, silencing its expression and promoting OC development. H3K18la reprograms MTHFD2 activity, increasing S-adenosylmethionine biosynthesis, and this process enhances the DNA methylation-dependent transcriptional silencing of SPINT2 , promoting OC progression. The results revealed a significant link between lactate metabolism reprogramming and epigenetic regulation, suggesting a new lactylation-based therapeutic strategy for OC patients.

title: AP2M1 promotes TNBC progression by stabilizing EGFR through inhibition of lysosomal degradation
abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive and heterogeneous malignancy, with 50–80% of cases exhibiting elevated EGFR expression. Dysregulated endocytic trafficking contributes to sustained receptor signaling and tumor progression, suggesting endocytosis as a potential therapeutic target. Transcriptome analysis of paired TNBC and adjacent tissues, together with public database analyses, identified AP2M1 as an endocytosis-related gene upregulated in TNBC tissues and cell lines. Functional assays, including proliferation, migration, and xenograft tumorigenicity, demonstrated that AP2M1 promotes TNBC progression. Mechanistically, in TNBC cells, AP2M1 interacts with EGFR, and its silencing accelerates EGFR internalization, enhances K63-linked ubiquitination, promotes EGFR trafficking to late endosomes, and facilitates lysosomal degradation, thereby reducing EGFR stability. Clinically, high AP2M1 expression is associated with poor prognosis in breast cancer. These findings indicate that AP2M1 stabilizes EGFR by inhibiting its lysosomal degradation, and that targeting the AP2M1–EGFR axis may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for EGFR-high TNBC.

title: ABE-mediated dual targeting of TOX and ARHGEF1 synergistically enhances antitumor activity of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes in PDAC
abstract: Tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) represent a promising immunotherapeutic modality in solid tumors, yet their clinical efficacy in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains severely limited by inefficient expansion and functional exhaustion. TILs were isolated from pancreatic cancer surgical specimens and were found to exhibit progressive functional impairment under sustained tumor exposure. Accordingly, we employed adenine base editing (ABE) to selectively target multiple exhaustion-associated genes in TILs. We found that concurrent knockdown of TOX and ARHGEF1 exerted a pronounced synergistic effect, characterized by significantly enhanced cytokine production, reduced expression of exhaustion markers such as PD-1 and TIM-3, and improved T-cell proliferative capacity. Functionally, dual TOX/ARHGEF1 knockdown increased the cytotoxic activity of TILs against matched tumor organoids and resulted in superior antitumor efficacy in vivo. Mechanistic investigations further indicated that this functional enhancement was closely associated with augmented IL-21 signaling and elevated STAT3 phosphorylation in gene-edited TILs. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that ABE-mediated co-targeting of TOX and ARHGEF1 effectively alleviates TIL functional exhaustion and enhances antitumor activity in PDAC, providing mechanistic insight and translational rationale for optimizing gene-engineered TIL-based immunotherapies.

title: Correction: NRF2 signaling plays an essential role in cancer progression through the NRF2-GPX2-NOTCH3 axis in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
abstract: Following the publication of this article, the authors noted an error in Figure 2F. Specifically, an incorrect representative Transwell invasion image was inadvertently used for the sgCtrl group in Figure 2F during figure preparation. We have replaced the incorrect image in Figure 2F with the correct representative image from the original experiment, as shown below. This correction is limited to the representative image and does not affect the underlying quantitative data, statistical analyses, interpretation, and conclusions of the article. The authors apologise for the error.

title: Meeting Report of the 6th edition of metabolism and cancer symposium
abstract: The 6th International Meeting "Metabolism and Cancer" was held at the Convention Center in La Grande Motte, France, on October 8-10, 2025. The three-day conference brought together 240 participants from eleven countries and featured 29 scientific presentations, including 15 invited lectures delivered by leading investigators in the field of oncometabolism. The program was structured into four thematic sessions: (i) diet, cachexia, microbiome, and microenvironment; (ii) stem cells and metabolic plasticity; (iii) epigenetics, epitranscriptomics, and metabolism; and (iv) metabolic control of drug resistance, therapy, and biomarkers. This meeting report highlights key conceptual advances and emerging directions discussed during the conference. Future progress in cancer metabolism will depend on elucidating the cross-talk between tumors and peripheral tissues, as organism-level metabolic regulation is likely to critically influence tumor growth, plasticity, and treatment sensitivity. Moving forward, a systems-level integration of metabolic, genomic, and spatial data is poised to redefine cancer metabolism from a descriptive field into a source of actionable vulnerabilities for precision oncology.

title: SMPD3 enhances MHC-I surface presentation to drive CD8⁺ T-cell immunity in colorectal cancer
abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is frequently accompanied by dysregulation of lipid metabolism. However, how sphingolipid metabolism–associated regulators influence key cellular processes in CRC remains unclear. By integrating TCGA and GEO datasets with differential expression analysis and machine learning, we identified SMPD3 as a candidate regulator of CRC progression and antitumor immunity. SMPD3 was downregulated in CRC tissues, whereas higher SMPD3 expression was associated with earlier-stage disease and improved survival. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis and immunohistochemistry further showed that high SMPD3 expression was associated with increased intratumoral CD8⁺ T-cell infiltration. In immunocompetent syngeneic mouse models, Smpd3 overexpression suppressed tumor growth and increased intratumoral CD8⁺ T-cell accumulation, and this antitumor effect depended on an immunocompetent host environment. SMPD3-high CRCs also exhibited higher PD-1-related immunophenoscores and a more favorable response pattern in a retrospective cohort receiving anti-PD-1-based therapy. Consistently, Smpd3 overexpression combined with anti-PD-1 treatment produced the lowest tumor burden in syngeneic CRC models. Mechanistically, SMPD3 enhanced cell-surface MHC-I presentation without substantially altering total MHC-I protein abundance. B2m knockdown reduced MHC-I surface expression and attenuated SMPD3-associated CD8⁺ T-cell-mediated cytotoxicity and tumor suppression, supporting the functional involvement of the B2m/MHC-I antigen-presentation axis. Brefeldin A blockade and washout assays further implicated intracellular trafficking in SMPD3-mediated MHC-I surface presentation, and SMPD3 may exert its antitumor immune effects through an intracellular mode of action. Together, these findings identify SMPD3 as a tumor-intrinsic regulator linking MHC-I surface presentation to CD8⁺ T-cell antitumor immunity and support its further evaluation as a candidate biomarker for PD-1 blockade responsiveness in CRC. SMPD3 enhances tumor cell-surface MHC-I availability through a B2m/MHC-I-dependent and trafficking-sensitive intracellular process, thereby promoting CD8⁺ T-cell-mediated antitumor immunity and supporting improved PD-1-related immune responsiveness in colorectal cancer.

title: Macrophage-mediated extracellular matrix remodeling awakens dormant breast cancer cells
abstract: Abstract Breast cancer recurrence remains a major cause of patient mortality. Recurrence arises from disseminated cancer cells that persist in a dormant state and can remain quiescent for extended periods before re-entering proliferation. Despite the clinical importance of this phenomenon, the cellular and molecular mechanisms that govern the awakening of dormant cancer cells remain incompletely understood. Inflammation has been extensively implicated in cancer progression; however, whether and how macrophages contribute to the awakening of dormant breast cancer cells is unclear. Using three-dimensional coculture systems, we show that macrophages promote the awakening of dormant breast cancer cells by remodeling the extracellular matrix (ECM), in vitro. We identify macrophage-derived matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP9) and lysyl oxidase (LOX) as key mediators of ECM remodeling, which in turn induces dormant cancer cell awakening. Mechanistically, macrophage-dependent ECM modifications trigger ligand-independent activation of EGFR/HER2 signaling in dormant cancer cells. Together, these findings establish a direct link between inflammation, ECM remodeling, and dormant cell awakening, revealing a previously unrecognized macrophage-cancer cell crosstalk that contributes to breast cancer recurrence.

title: Metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming as novel vulnerabilities in renal cell carcinoma
abstract: Renal Cell Carcinomas (RCCs) are metabolically heterogeneous tumors with distinct genetic, epigenetic, and metabolic alterations. In clear cell Renal Cell Carcinoma, VHL gene loss leads to stabilization of Hypoxia Inducible Factors (HIF1α and HIF2α), promoting angiogenesis and metabolic reprogramming enhancing cellular energy production. Papillary Renal Cell Carcinoma, frequently harboring mutations in Tricarboxylic Acid cycle enzymes (FH, SDH), results in the accumulation of different “oncometabolites”, capable to drive pseudohypoxia and epigenetic dysregulation. Chromophobe Renal Cell Carcinoma is instead associated with mitochondrial defects and limited glycolytic activity. In this context, a tight interplay exists between metabolism and the epigenetic landscape. Oncometabolites are able to inhibit key chromatin-modifying enzymes, altering gene expression and promoting tumorigenesis. RCCs also exhibits frequent mutations in epigenetic regulators, further contributing to metabolic rewiring and tumor progression. Inhibiting oncometabolite accumulation, disrupting amino acid metabolism, modulating lipid anabolic routes, or targeting epigenetic enzymes could complement current treatments. Understanding the metabolic dependencies of RCC cells may lead to the development of novel, personalized therapies.

title: Co-targeting ASAH1 and the histone reader BRD1 potently suppresses TNBC growth through the transcriptional repressor BCL6
abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is a highly aggressive breast cancer subtype with limited targeted therapeutic options, leading to higher mortality rates compared to other breast cancer subtypes. In our previous study, we identified that N-acyl sphingosine amidohydrolase 1 (ASAH1) is overexpressed in TNBC cells, and its genetic and pharmacological targeting suppresses TNBC growth and progression. In the current study, we performed a small-molecule screen using epigenetic inhibitors in combination with the ASAH1 inhibitor carmofur to identify potential epigenetic regulators that can be co-targeted to enhance the antitumor effect of carmofur. We identified the bromodomain containing protein 1 (BRD1) inhibitors (BAY-299, NI57 and OF1), which when combined with carmofur led to stronger inhibition of TNBC tumor growth in cell culture and in in vivo model compared to either single agent alone. Mechanistically, BAY-299 in combination with carmofur induced higher expression of the transcriptional repressor B-cell lymphoma 6 (BCL6), resulting in stronger inhibition of the anti-apoptotic gene, B-cell lymphoma 2 (BCL2) than either treatment alone. This consequently led to enhanced apoptosis in TNBC cells treated with both BAY-299 and carmofur. Collectively, these results identify a previously undocumented therapeutic combination of BRD1 inhibitors and ASAH1 inhibitor carmofur as a promising treatment strategy for TNBC.

title: Correction to: Paladin, overexpressed in colon cancer, is required for actin polymerisation and liver metastasis dissemination
abstract: Following publication of this article an error was noted in Fig. 2a, specifically an inadvertent duplication in the red Ponceau bands of samples from Patient # 8 and Patient # 10.
